# The Willpower Method

> "For I don't practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do."
>
> — Romans 7:15

Everybody knows that stopping is hard. The forums say so. The apps say so. The men's breakfast at church says so, and adds that you'll be fighting this until the day you die. Nearly every book on the subject opens by warning you what a brutal road lies ahead.

The truth is that it's absurdly easy.

I know how that sounds. Bear with me. If I told you to run a marathon in under three hours, that would be hard. You'd need years of training, and you might not have the legs for it however hard you trained. But stopping the habit doesn't ask you to *do* anything. You only have to not do something. Nobody is holding you down and making you. Your body doesn't need it the way it needs bread and water. So if you want to stop, where exactly is the difficulty?

There isn't one. Men create the difficulty themselves, by using the Willpower Method. I mean any way of quitting that leaves you feeling you've sacrificed something. Let's look at how it goes.

## How we got here {-}

None of us decided to become a man who does this every night. We tried it once out of curiosity, and it was honestly nothing much: over quickly and a bit embarrassing. For that very reason we felt sure we could take it or leave it.

For a while we could. It was now and then, when the mood took us. Then, without any decision, it was most nights. Then it had its own slots in the day: the shower, the bed, the empty house. Then we wouldn't have known how to get to sleep without it. Somewhere along the way we came to feel we were *owed* it, as a man's rightful release and his one reward for a hard day. We never noticed that it had stopped delivering even the little it once did. The same memories went stale, and the mind had to reach further each time to raise a flicker.

It usually takes years to realise you're hooked, because of one stubborn illusion: we assume men do this because they enjoy it. So on the nights we plainly don't enjoy it, we conclude we could stop any time. "I don't even like it that much. I could drop it tomorrow." That's the confidence trap. Somehow tomorrow is never the day you want to.

The problem only shows itself when we actually try. The first attempt tends to come early. A girl appears and you want to be better for her. A sermon lands. You come home from a retreat, or it's New Year, or it's simply the morning after a night that left you sick of yourself.

## The first attempts {-}

Notice when it is that a man makes his attempt. Whatever sets it off, it's nearly always a bad moment: he's ashamed, rattled, and already under strain.

He stops. Within a day or two the Little Monster is hungry and he wants his comfort. But he's sworn off his comfort. So now he has the original strain, plus the itch, plus the fact that the one thing he's always used to settle himself is forbidden. That's three blows at once.

He holds out through a few grim days of this, and then he does a deal. "I'll cut down." "I picked a bad week." "I'll do it properly once this deadline's over." Then the deadline passes, the pressure lifts, and with it goes any reason to stop. He won't think about quitting again until the next bad patch. Life doesn't run out of those. There are exams, then a job, then a mortgage, then small children and aging parents. The quiet season he's waiting for is not on the calendar. (And the habit itself keeps him a notch more on edge than he need be, but that's for a later chapter.)

After a few failures of this kind, a man generally falls back on hope. One morning, he tells himself, he'll just wake up and not want it any more. That is Augustine's prayer from an earlier chapter, the one he wrote down to his own shame: chastity, "only not yet." He knew the prayer was a stall, and later he mocked his own delay: "tomorrow, and tomorrow?"

The hope gets fed by stories. "My cousin just stopped. Got married and never thought about it again." Don't be fooled. Look into those stories and they're never that simple. Either the man had been working up to it for a year and the wedding was the last push, or he'd had a fright. His wife found something, or his body failed him at the wrong moment. No man has ever drifted out of this trap by accident. **IT WON'T HAPPEN UNLESS YOU MAKE IT HAPPEN.**

## Why willpower is so hard {-}

Let's slow down and watch the Willpower Method work.

For most of our lives we take the ostrich line: "I'll sort it out later." Every so often something jolts us into an attempt. So we sit down and add it up. On one side go the shame, the tiredness, the wasted hours, the distance from God and the look we can't give our wife. On the other side goes… what, exactly? Any honest tally comes out the same, and it has done since we were fifteen: **STOP. YOU'RE BEING A FOOL.**

So he knows he'd be better off without it. That was never in doubt. What trips him is something else: he believes he's making a sacrifice. He can't say what it is he's sacrificing. He only has a feeling that in the good times and the bad times alike, the habit *helps*. It's an illusion, but it's a strong one.

On top of that sit the lies about the habit that he's soaked up from the world, and on top of those sits the heaviest lie of all, which is how terrible it is to quit. He's heard about the man ninety days clean who still thinks about it every hour. He's heard about the old saint who says he's battled it for fifty years. He's read about the man who set himself five years, reached day 280, and lost it in one lonely evening. He may know one or two men who are obviously being eaten by this and still can't stop. Most likely he's lived some of those stories himself.

So he doesn't start out thinking, "Wonderful! Have you heard? I don't have to do this any more!" He starts in dread, like a man looking up at a north face. He texts his accountability partner: "Pray for me. This month is going to be rough." Most attempts are beaten before they begin.

A psychiatrist who treats porn addiction has watched where the fighting leads: "the more you fight the more you fail and the more you fail the more your brain is learning we're not going to win this might as well give up". He gives the reason too: "willpower is a diminishing resource so the more you use it the less you have to resist".

Suppose he gets through the first few days. He feels a bit brighter. There's a little more spring in the mornings. And the reasons that made him stop are already fading. It's like passing a pile-up on the motorway. You ease off for ten miles, shaken, and by the time you're running late again your foot is back on the floor.

Meanwhile the Little Monster hasn't been fed. There's no pain in it. If a head cold made you feel like that, you wouldn't even mention it. But he knows what he wants. So the Little Monster wakes the Big Monster, and now watch something remarkable. The very man who three days ago was listing every reason to stop starts hunting, just as earnestly, for a reason to start:

- "Life's short. I could be dead by Friday. There are worse sins."
- "I chose the wrong week."
- "I should have waited until after the holidays / the exams / the move."
- "I can't think straight. I'm snapping at everyone. I can't do my job like this."
- "I'm unbearable to live with. For my family's sake I ought to just get it over with."
- "It isn't even mentioned in the Bible."
- "Better this than going back to porn."
- "God made men this way. He can't expect the impossible."
- "It's been a week and I feel nothing down there. I'd better check everything still works."

This is the point where he gives in.

What follows is the strangest minute of all. He feels real relief, because the Little Monster has been fed and has stopped nagging. In the same minute there's the flatness, and the old question: *why did I do that?* He draws the obvious conclusion that he's weak and has no willpower.

It wasn't weakness. He changed his mind. Given what he believed at that moment, that he was suffering, that the habit would end the suffering, and that there was something in it for him after all, going back was a perfectly logical decision. His will was fine. He was acting on false information.

"What's the point of a clean conscience if I'm miserable?" None at all! If a life without the habit really were grey and twitchy, I'd tell you to forget the whole thing. It isn't. But notice where his misery comes from. It doesn't come from the Little Monster, who is a pipsqueak. It comes from the tug-of-war. He starts by believing he's given something up, so he feels deprived, and feeling deprived is itself a strain. In a strain, the old voice says "go on", and now he can't. So he feels more deprived still.

## The counter {-}

One feature of the Willpower Method makes it worse than everything else, and the modern version has built it into an app.

If you're training for a driving test, you know the moment you've succeeded, because the examiner hands you a slip of paper. On the Willpower Method there's no slip of paper. The plan is: "If I can just go long enough without it, the wanting will stop." How long is long enough? Nobody can tell you. So you count.

The big online movement has made a liturgy of this. There are day counters, badges, and a ninety-day target that its own site describes as "difficult for most, yet achievable." When a man falls, he performs the rite the site calls a reset: "Resetting means restarting their challenge beginning with day one and starting again."

Think about what a counter actually measures. It measures the distance between you and the last time you did it. So every morning it points you back at the habit, the very thing you're trying to leave behind. A man with a streak thinks about masturbation more than a man without one. He has to. He's keeping score.

One man, who now teaches other men about this, lived on two-week streaks for years until he saw what was wrong with them: "I realized something that I was obsessing over my sin." He drew the lesson in one line: "What you set your gaze upon will disciple you." A counter sets your gaze on the habit every morning.

Scroll down under any video on this subject and you'll find the same rite in the comments, posted again and again by different men: "Day 1 of quitting." Then today's date. Then "Like this comment so I always get reminders!" Each man means it with his whole heart, and each has asked a crowd of strangers to remind him, every time they press a button, of the thing he's trying to forget. Under one such video an older hand left the right advice: "You need to stop 'keeping scores' as a way to gauge how delivered you are."

And who counts days? A man scratching lines on a cell wall counts days. A free man has no idea how many days it's been since he was released. He's got better things to do. I couldn't tell you how long it's been since I last bit my nails. Each number on that counter says "day forty of doing without", and a man who's doing without has decided in advance that he's losing something.

Then there's the reset. One slip on day sixty-one and the screen says zero. All of it gone! So what does the man at zero do? More often than not he thinks, "Well, it's ruined now," and makes a weekend of it before starting the count again on Monday. The counter turned one bad night into three. A man who had quit for good and stumbled would pick himself up the same hour. The man with a counter has to start again from the bottom of the hill.

One veteran of those forums saw what it does to people and left a warning: "Don't be in perpetual recovery, or become a serial-relapser." A streak makes exactly that kind of man. He's permanently on day something, and he never gets to be simply free.

So the man on the Willpower Method waits. And while he waits, the questions come:

- "How long is this going to last?"
- "Will I ever enjoy a quiet evening again?"
- "Will I ever sleep properly?"
- "What will I do the next time everything goes wrong?"

He's waiting for things to get better, and while he mopes, the thing he's given up grows more precious by the day. The miserable men on those forums aren't suffering from withdrawal. What hurts them is doubt.

## The honest man in Romans 7 {-}

If you want the Willpower Method described by someone who wasn't selling an app, read Paul.

"For the good which I desire, I don't do; but the evil which I don't desire, that I practice." (Romans 7:19)

That is as honest a sentence as any man has written about himself. And Paul was no weakling. He was beaten, shipwrecked and stoned, and he kept going. If grit were the cure, he had more of it than you or I ever will. Yet when his own will went up against his own flesh, he lost, and he said so.

Augustine was caught in the same place three centuries later. You've read his account of the chain, and of the iron will that forged it. A little further on comes the line every man on a streak will recognise: "Thus did my two wills, one new, and the other old, one carnal, the other spiritual, struggle within me; and by their discord, undid my soul."

Two wills. That's what you've been living with. One of them wants to be free and the other wants one more night. The Willpower Method is the plan of setting the first to overpower the second, every day, for good. But it's all one man. You're arm-wrestling yourself, and whichever arm wins, you're the one who's tired. The men who've tried it will tell you:

> "I've fasted and I've prayed but is even worst now"
>
> — a commenter on a Christian recovery blog

The same man, a day earlier: "I've tried al that I cn possibly do to stop but it's al in vain it's been 6 years now." And a nineteen-year-old on another site:

> "Every time I failed to shake the affliction I became more and more depressed and my faith was severely stunted."
>
> — a testimony on a Christian site

A young man who told his story to a camera said what the end of every attempt looked like: "no matter how much willpower that I've had", it always finished the same way, with "me on my bed disgusted with myself". And a commenter, in a line thousands of men endorsed: "Every time I think I've escaped this sin, it comes back at me like a bite of a snake."

These men aren't lazy and they aren't faithless. They tried as hard as anyone could, and trying harder was the one thing that couldn't work.

Now look at how Paul ends the chapter. "What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!" (Romans 7:24–25)

His question isn't "*how* shall I try harder?" It's "*who* will deliver me?" The answer is a person and a gift, and it comes with a shout of thanks. He never mentions a technique. The old Puritan John Owen spent a whole book on killing sin and was nobody's idea of a soft touch, and he said the same thing: "All other ways of mortification are vain, all helps leave us helpless; it must be done by the Spirit." He put it more vividly in another place: "A man may easier see without eyes, speak without a tongue, than truly mortify one sin without the Spirit." Even a coach who preaches discipline for a living tells his young men, "your willpower will fail you every single time."

If you're not a believer, stay with me, because the logic holds without the theology: the war between two wills doesn't end when one of them finally wins. **IT ENDS WHEN ONE OF THEM IS GONE.** The will that wants "one more night" lives entirely on the belief that the night has something to offer. Take away the belief and there's no second will left to fight. That's what this book is doing, a chapter at a time.

## Meanwhile, on day forty {-}

Back to our man on his streak, because something really is happening to him, though he can't feel it. If he lasts a few weeks, the Little Monster starves. The bodily itch is so slight that he never notices it die.

Around then he feels he's cracked it. So he allows himself one, to prove the point, or to celebrate, or just to see. He does it, and it's a let-down, as it always was. But the Little Monster has had a meal, and next day there's a small voice asking for another. He had been out, and he's walked back in.

He doesn't go straight back to nightly. He's careful and leaves it a week or two. Then he reasons, "I had one and didn't get hooked, so one more is safe." That's the same reasoning he used at thirteen, and it works the same way now.

Think of a small boy with a comfort blanket. One mother hides it on top of the wardrobe. Her son cries for a week, and for a year afterwards he still looks up at the wardrobe. Another mother simply waits until her son is seven, when he looks at the grubby rag one day and can't think what he ever saw in it. Nobody needs willpower to do without a comfort blanket at thirty. The Willpower Method puts the blanket on the wardrobe. This book wants you to look at it.

Some men do succeed on willpower. I don't want to take anything away from them. But listen to how they tell it. It was long and it was bitter, because the lie was still in their heads the whole time. The Little Monster had been dead for months and they were still moping. At last it dawned on them that they weren't going to give in, the moping stopped, and they found that life went on perfectly well.

Many more fail than succeed that way. And some who succeed stay fragile for the rest of their lives, because a corner of them still believes the habit had something to give. That's why a man can be ten years clear and fall in one bad week. One commenter put all of it into a single line: "I thought I had Kicked the habit but the habit came back."

Others keep the odd one as "a treat", or as a test of how strong they've become. The test passes. And the moment it's over, a small voice starts lobbying for the next. "Well, I didn't enjoy that much, so I'm clearly in no danger. After Christmas I'll knock it off entirely."

By then it's too late, and the trap he fought his way out of has him again.

## Enjoyment never came into it {-}

I'll say again what I said earlier, because everything hangs on it. Enjoyment has nothing to do with this, and it never did. If men did it for enjoyment, they wouldn't do it when they're ill, or exhausted, or an hour after they'd promised God. We only assume we enjoy it because the alternative is too insulting to consider: that we've been doing something for twenty years that gives us nothing.

That's also why most of it happens half-asleep, on autopilot, in the dark. Watch a man at this habit, if such a thing could be watched, and you'd see he's only content while he isn't thinking about what he's doing. The moment he thinks about it, he's uneasy.

Remember the thread running through this book: a man who can't control his lust can't be trusted. The Willpower Method agrees with that sentence and then gets the cure wrong. It thinks self-control means holding a door shut for the rest of your life against something heavy leaning on the other side. That isn't self-control. It's a siege, and sooner or later the man inside gets tired.

Real self-control looks different. There's nothing leaning on the door. The man opens it and shuts it as he pleases, and half the time he forgets it's there.

The habit feeds the Little Monster. The lies are the Big Monster. Starve the first, clear out the second, and you will have **NEITHER THE NEED NOR THE WISH** to masturbate again.
